hero.name: Arvind
hero.who: a supermarket cashier in Vadodara, newly promoted to floor manager and unsure of his job

story.h: The fastest cashier, now a manager
story.b: For six years Arvind was the fastest billing cashier at a busy supermarket in Vadodara. Customers queued at his counter on purpose. Last month he was promoted to floor manager, in charge of eleven staff across billing, stocking and the fresh section. Now his days feel strange. Whenever queues grow, he jumps behind a counter, because that is what he is good at. Meanwhile shelves sit half-empty, a new stocker keeps pushing older stock to the back, and two cashiers argue about shifts. At night he feels he worked hard, yet the store manager calls the week messy. Arvind honestly does not know what a manager is supposed to produce.

ask.q: Arvind keeps billing customers himself when things get busy. What should he understand about his new role?
o: His job is to be the hardest worker on the floor, setting an example
His output is now what his whole team achieves, not just his own billing
He should go back to cashier work, since that is his real strength
ask.why: Billing feels productive, but one fast cashier cannot fix empty shelves and team fights. Going back avoids the real job. As a manager, his results are what the whole floor produces, so his time should go into making all eleven people more effective.

chapters.take: A manager's output is the team's output, not their own task list.

story.b: Navratri week arrives, the busiest of the year. On the first evening the billing queues stretch to the biscuit aisle. Arvind's hands itch to jump onto a counter. Instead he stands back and looks at the whole floor. He moves one stocker who used to be a cashier to open a fourth counter. He asks the fresh section to pre-pack sweets in half-kilo boxes, so billing goes faster. He settles the shift argument with a simple rotation chart. That night he writes down what the team achieved, not what he did: more bills than last Navratri, no empty snack shelves, nobody storming out in anger. For the first time, the store manager calls the week smooth.

ask.q: On a busy Sunday, deputy Hetal starts filling an empty shelf herself while a new stocker stands idle. What should she do?
o: Show the stocker how to fill it, so the floor gains another working pair of hands
Fill the shelf herself, since she is faster than the new boy
Leave the shelf empty until the morning team arrives
ask.why: Doing it herself fixes one shelf but leaves the stocker idle and the next shelf empty too. Waiting until morning loses sales. Getting the stocker working raises what the whole team produces, which is the real measure of a manager's day.

chapters.take: Judge your day by what your team got done, not by your own busyness.

story.b: Arvind looks at how he spends his hours. Two hours a day go into supplier meetings where he only listens. Another hour goes into answering the same staff questions again and again. Almost nothing goes into training. So he tries a different split. He spends thirty minutes teaching Sahil, the new stocker, how to rotate stock so older items go to the front. He pins next week's roster on the board every Thursday instead of announcing it on Sunday night. He sends his deputy to two of the supplier meetings. Within two weeks, expired-stock losses drop, staff stop calling him about shifts, and Arvind has an hour a day he did not have before.

ask.q: Arvind has one free hour today. Which use has the most leverage?
o: Sitting in another supplier meeting just to be seen there
Billing at a counter to shorten the queue for an hour
Training two new cashiers on the system so they work faster for months
ask.why: An hour at the counter helps only that hour, and a meeting where he adds nothing helps nobody. Training two cashiers well improves their work every shift for months, so the same hour multiplies across many days and many customers. That is high leverage.

chapters.take: Spend your hours where they multiply across many people.

story.h: The chart on the fridge door
story.b: One Monday, a customer returns spoiled paneer and complains loudly at the counter. Arvind discovers the dairy fridge has been running warm since Saturday, and nobody noticed. Half the stock has to be thrown away. Instead of only scolding the dairy staff, he asks where the problem could have been caught earlier and cheaply. He tapes a small chart to the fridge door, where the opening staff note the temperature at eight and at two. He also asks for a short list every morning of items within three days of expiry, so they can go on discount early. Two weeks later the chart shows the temperature creeping up one afternoon. A technician fixes a loose door seal before anything spoils.

ask.q: Arvind wants to stop wrong prices from reaching customers. Where is the best place to catch these errors?
o: At the billing counter, when customers point out the mistakes
When new price tags go up each morning, with a quick spot-check
At the end of the month, when the accounts team checks losses
ask.why: Catching errors at billing means an annoyed customer has already found them, and a monthly check finds them weeks too late. A quick check when tags go up catches problems at the earliest and cheapest stage, before they cost money or trust.

chapters.take: Catch problems at the earliest, cheapest stage, before they grow expensive.

story.b: Arvind starts a simple habit: a twenty-minute chat every two weeks with each person on his team, over chai in the storeroom. He tells them it is their time. They bring the topics, and he mostly listens and asks questions. The first few chats are awkward. Then people open up. Komal, a cashier, mentions that the scanner at counter three freezes every evening, which explains the long queues there. Bhavin from the fresh section suggests selling pre-cut vegetables for office-goers. Sahil admits he cannot read the expiry codes on imported goods. Each chat takes twenty minutes and saves hours of confusion later. Arvind starts to look forward to them.

ask.q: In a one-on-one, Komal sits quietly, and Arvind is tempted to fill the time with instructions. What should he do?
o: Ask open questions and let her set the topics, listening more than talking
Use the time to list everything she should improve
Cancel her chats, since she clearly has nothing to say
ask.why: Filling the time with instructions turns it into a lecture, and cancelling misses what she may be hesitant to share. These chats work when the team member leads and the manager listens. A few open questions often uncover problems and ideas that would otherwise stay hidden.

chapters.take: Regular one-on-ones, led by your team member, catch problems before they explode.

story.h: Closing the cash for the first time
story.b: A month later, Arvind asks Komal to handle the evening cash closing, a task she has never done. On billing she needs no supervision at all, so he almost leaves her alone with the closing too. Then he reminds himself that experience belongs to the task, not the person. For the first week he sits with her, walks her through each step and checks her totals. By the second week he only checks the final sheet. Meanwhile Hetal, his deputy, has planned Diwali stock twice before. With her he does the opposite: a short check-in every Friday and full freedom in between. Sahil still gets clear daily steps on new tasks, and a lighter touch on the ones he has mastered.

ask.q: Hetal has planned festive stock for years but has never handled hiring. How should Arvind manage her first hiring task?
o: Give her full freedom, since she is experienced and capable
Give clear guidance and closer support, since hiring is new for her
Do the hiring himself, since she has never done it before
ask.why: Her experience with stock does not transfer to hiring, so full freedom could leave her stuck or making avoidable mistakes. Taking it over means she never learns. Closer guidance on this new task, while keeping her freedom on stock planning, fits his support to her experience with each job.

chapters.take: Match how closely you manage to a person's experience with that specific task.

story.h: Diwali, from the back of the floor
story.b: By Diwali, Arvind's floor runs differently. He rarely stands behind a counter now, and the queues are shorter anyway, because the scanner at counter three was replaced and two new cashiers were trained well. The fridge chart gets filled twice a day without reminders. Pre-cut vegetables sell out by seven each evening. Komal handles the closing alone. The storeroom chai chats continue, and the problems they bring up keep getting smaller. The store manager asks Arvind to train two new floor managers from other branches. On the first day, one of them asks how he finds time to do everything. Arvind smiles and says he no longer tries to do everything. He helps everyone else do it.

chapters.take: A good manager multiplies the team instead of trying to outwork it.
